parsed.explanation: The combined national and division regime is hostile at every traveller-facing stage. National visa and passport rules can refuse or permanently bar applicants whose sex markers or records appear discrepant; the division confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in all public buildings including airports, imposes fines and private bounty suits, and invalidates nonmatching state IDs. A pending lawsuit and a public-accommodations law do not neutralize the operative facility ban. National custody and counterterrorism rhetoric add severe risk if identity is discovered in detention. No execution or routine imprisonment for trans status is documented, keeping the score above the 0.15 tier, but universal facility exposure and entry refusal place it in High Risk.

entry_documents.exposure: National visa and passport rules bar self-selected markers, halt new X markers, and instruct refusal where documents cast doubt on sex; suspected misrepresentation can support permanent fraud ineligibility. Trans travellers report blocked or confiscated passports and stranded trips.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; a fraud finding requires four elements and is not automatic; litigation challenges the passport policy.
entry_documents.interaction: A visitor with an X or mismatched marker may be refused at visa or entry; division ID invalidation adds domestic document friction at airports and public buildings.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Border discrepancy can escalate to secondary inspection or refusal; national immigration custody documents forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse of trans men; corrections policy imposes conversion practices and denies hormones.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Fraud finding is not automatic; limited waiver possibilities exist; courts have enjoined some national orders; a legal-aid FAQ exists.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Document mismatch can move to refusal or detention, then birth-sex custody and care denial; no division-specific visitor remedy is documented.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Division law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in all publicly owned buildings including airports, schools and government offices; civil and criminal penalties reach $1,000; any private person may sue for at least $1,000; nonmatching licences are invalidated.
federal_state_facilities.protection: State public-accommodations law covers gender identity; two trans men sued; no injunction is recorded.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Airport or public-building use by an outed traveller carries bounty and penalty regardless of residence; airport transit is the sharpest visitor exposure.

care_services.exposure: National policy calls minor gender-affirming care mutilation, restricts funding and insurance, and custody denies hormones; the division bans minor care, subject to a May 2026 injunction. Adult visitor care is not documented.
care_services.protection: The division injunction blocks the minor-care ban; state public-accommodations law applies; no explicit traveller care protection is documented.
care_services.interaction: A trans minor needing care faces denial; an adult traveller’s medication or care can expose identity at the border or a clinic with no documented visitor remedy.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy prioritizes ‘radically pro-transgender’ groups; a justice reward system targets domestic terrorists; executive orders target gender ideology and school support for trans minors.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The memo says the reward phrase is not a criterion; counterterrorism powers are stated not to target mere disagreement; several orders are enjoined; national hate-crime law covers gender identity.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official framing raises the risk that police or border attention treats trans identity as security-adjacent, but no visitor prosecution solely for status is documented.

minors_guardians.exposure: The division facility and ID law reaches minors in public buildings; national order threatens prosecution of teachers who affirm trans minors; minor care bans exist in the division and national proposals. A parent with a trans minor faces the same airport and facility bounty exposure.
minors_guardians.protection: The division minor-care ban was enjoined in May 2026; a parental lawsuit exists; no parent-targeted visitor penalty is documented.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans minor cannot avoid public-building facilities and may be outed with a guardian; care needs add exposure, but visitor-specific enforcement is not documented.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No trans-specific violence rate is documented; the division hate-crime law omits gender identity; the bounty incentivizes private reporting; public-opinion majorities back birth-sex document and sports rules.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity since 2009; state public-accommodations law applies; police response is not documented.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Thin state recourse and bounty reporting can turn public confrontation into civil or official action; national coverage may not reach local police practice.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The facility-bounty lawsuit is unresolved; enforcement and suit counts are unsourced; licence invalidation notices are ongoing; passport litigation is unresolved. Visitor remedies against bounty or refusal are not documented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties litigation, a legal-aid FAQ, court blocks on some national orders, and existing X passports valid until expiry.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Protections are prospective and partial; the operative division ban and national entry rules remain in force, leaving travellers uncertain.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.25-A has coercive custody, extortion and threatened imprisonment but no state-imposed facility ban. This dossier lacks documented routine visitor custody or extortion, yet its universal public-building facility exclusion with a private bounty and ID invalidation is a tier-1 exposure, so it sits at or slightly below 0.25-A rather than above it.

0.35-A documents denial of entry and invasive administrative review but no detention and no facility ban. This regime adds a bounty-backed birth-sex facility rule in airports and public buildings plus possible permanent visa ineligibility, so it is materially less safe than 0.35-A.

0.55-B has an operative protection that resolves an ID discrepancy after delay, with no detention. Here entry refusal and facility penalties are operative, remedies are pending, and the division is flagged Do Not Travel; the case is far below 0.55-B.

0.15-A involves standard severe imprisonment and unresolved capital possibility. Here no execution or routine imprisonment for trans status is documented, only denial of entry, fines, bounty suits and dangerous custody if detained, so this case is above 0.15-A.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is national entry and document screening layered onto a division facility ban. At the border, an X or mismatched marker can trigger refusal or fraud ineligibility; inside the division, any outed trans person using an airport or other public-building restroom is exposed to a $1,000 penalty and private bounty suit, and nonmatching state IDs are invalid. The state public-accommodations law and pending lawsuit do not suspend the ban. National custody and counterterrorism rhetoric make detention especially dangerous. Because no execution or routine imprisonment for trans status is documented, the case is above the 0.15 imprisonment tier, but universal facility exposure, bounty enforcement and entry refusal put it in High Risk.
